text.p: These are the leading stories in the Namibian press on Thursday.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- A fired-up President Sam Nujoma, gunning for a third term as head of state, on Wednesday launched yet another attack on the media in Namibia, telling them to "wake up" and to stop being "used by other interests".

- Namibia's most powerful union grouping, the National Union of Namibian Workers, on Wednesday night solidly threw its weight behind Deputy Prime Minister Hendrik Witbooi for the post of SWAPO vice president, a dominant issue at the ruling party's congress underway in Windhoek.

The NUNW, affiliated to SWAPO, alleged that "dirty campaign tactics", reminiscent of the Democratic Turnhalle Alliance, were being deployed in the contest which pits Witbooi agianst Prime Minster Hage Geingob for the post of vice presient of SWAPO.

- Namibia is still the Utopia for which President Sam Nujoma and other freedom fighters fought for 23 years. His Utopia is, however, a country where journalists don't deliver criticism but rather take their bags and go.

In his opening speech at the SWAPO congress, the president said he would continue with his plans to tap water from the Congo River for Namibia and Botswana, to use the rich fish resources and to combat desertification. But white journalists and the print media in general were not part of his greater plans.

- National airline Air Namibia is facing massive losses of N$47 million for 1997. With an audit of the company's books in full swing, the chairman of the Transnamib board of directors Willy Klein, on Wednesday hinted that the losses could be even higher than that. What was condemned as "mere rumours" a couple of months ago, now seem to be real, and the pressure from amongst others Lufthansa together with the weakening of the Namibian Dollar against the U.S. dollar are being given as the main reasons for the losses.

- President Sam Nujoma on Wednesday opened the SWAPO congress with a speech, which in essence, echoes what he said at the opneing of parliament and during his state of the nation address earlier this year. Concrete statements regarding the four-day congress were not made, and new revelations were only made where the president deviated from his prepared speech. In his 13-page statement the president once again gave detailed explanations on the successes of the first national development plan. But the economic growth of 3.6 percent, he said, remained meaningless if Namibia was not able to get rid of its chronic water shortage.
